claims.claim: For d=δ⁺(D)≥1, a directed cycle of length at least d+1 can be found in polynomial time; additionally, n<d+k is an immediate sound NO condition. Thus the target is completely solved for k=1.
claims.evidence: For a maximal simple directed path v₁…v_p, every out-neighbor of v_p lies earlier on the path. If v_i is the earliest such neighbor, the d distinct out-neighbors occupy positions i,…,p−1, so d≤p−i. Hence v_i…v_pv_i is a cycle of length p−i+1≥d+1. Greedy extension is polynomial. No cycle can exceed n, proving the NO rule; for k=1 the constructed cycle reaches d+k.
claims.witness: The maximal-path construction itself returns the required cycle.
claims.search_method: Direct extremal proof and exhaustive exact testing of every loopless digraph on 2–4 vertices.

claims.claim: For any integer L≥2, existence of a directed cycle of length at least L is exactly equivalent to a short-leg two-way linkage, yielding an explicit O(n^L(n+m)) exact algorithm.
claims.evidence: A qualifying cycle supplies L consecutive distinct vertices and its complementary return segment avoids the internal L−2 vertices. Conversely, an enumerated directed L-vertex path plus a simple return path in the graph with those internal vertices deleted forms a simple directed cycle of length at least L. There are at most n^L tuples, and each tuple requires O(n+m) reachability work; L>n is rejected immediately.
claims.witness: Concatenate an accepted tuple v₁…v_L with the reconstructed simple v_L-to-v₁ return path.
claims.search_method: Bidirectional proof of the equivalence, runtime accounting, and exhaustive exact comparison on every loopless digraph through four vertices.

claims.claim: There is a polynomially checkable upper-bound certificate: if X is an independent vertex set and every arc entering X from outside X has its tail in S⊆V(D)\X, then every directed cycle has length at most n−|X|+|S|.
claims.evidence: Each cycle vertex in X has a predecessor outside X because X is independent, and the entry hypothesis puts that predecessor in S. Different X-vertices have different predecessors because every vertex has only one successor on a directed cycle. Thus a cycle uses at most |S| vertices of X and at most n−|X| vertices outside X, giving the claimed bound. All hypotheses and the resulting inequality are polynomially checkable.
claims.witness: The injective map x↦the predecessor of x on the cycle certifies |C∩X|≤|S|.
claims.search_method: Direct injection proof plus exhaustive testing of 131755 eligible (D,X,S) certificates for digraphs through four vertices.

claims.claim: Let D be a bidirected complete multipartite digraph on n vertices, and let d=δ⁺(D). Its circumference is exactly min(n,2d), and a maximum directed cycle can be constructed in polynomial time. If d≥2, then D is 2-strong.
claims.evidence: If the largest part has size M, then d=n−M. Its cycle vertices must be separated by vertices outside that part, proving c(D)≤min(n,2d). When M>d, alternating all d outside vertices with d largest-part vertices gives a 2d-cycle. When M≤d, distribute every other part injectively among M gaps between largest-part vertices; empty-first distribution makes every gap nonempty, and each gap contains vertices from distinct parts, yielding a Hamiltonian cycle. If d≥2, deletion of any one vertex leaves at least two nonempty parts, and the remaining bidirected complete multipartite graph is strong.
claims.witness: The alternating construction realizes 2d when 2d<n; the nonempty-gap construction realizes n otherwise.
claims.search_method: Complete two-case proof, deletion analysis, and exact testing of all 65 integer part-size patterns of orders 2–8.

claims.claim: The target has a polynomial-time solution on bidirected complete multipartite digraphs: such an input is YES exactly when n≥d+k and d≥k.
claims.evidence: Using c(D)=min(n,2d), the target is feasible exactly when min(n,2d)≥d+k. This is equivalent to n≥d+k and 2d≥d+k, with the latter equivalent to d≥k. The maximum-cycle construction from claim 3 is polynomial and supplies a witness in every YES case.
claims.witness: The constructed cycle has length min(n,2d), which reaches d+k exactly under the two stated inequalities.
claims.search_method: Algebraic equivalence and exhaustive exact testing across multipartite part-size patterns and all relevant k.

claims.claim: For every fixed k≥3 there are 2-strong NO-instances of arbitrarily large order satisfying n≥d+k: the bidirected complete bipartite digraph with part sizes 2 and a, for any a≥k, has d=2 and circumference 4=d+2.
claims.evidence: In bidirected K_{2,a}, vertices in the a-part have outdegree 2 and those in the 2-part have outdegree a, so d=2. Every cycle alternates between parts and hence has length at most 4, while a directed 4-cycle exists. Deleting any one vertex leaves both parts nonempty for a≥3, so the remainder is strong. For a≥k≥3, n=a+2≥d+k while 4<d+k, and a is unbounded.
claims.witness: Any two vertices from each part form a directed 4-cycle; alternation proves it is maximum.
claims.search_method: Direct degree, alternation, connectivity, and inequality proof with exact parameter-grid checks.

claims.claim: For every fixed k≥4 there are 2-strong NO-instances with arbitrarily large minimum outdegree and with n≥d+k; indeed their circumference is exactly d+3.
claims.evidence: Take a bidirected q-clique Q with gateways x,y, an independent set A, all arcs A→Q, and only x,y sending arcs from Q to A. For q≥3, d=q−1. Every cycle uses at most two A-vertices because each requires a distinct predecessor in {x,y}, so its length is at most q+2=d+3. The cycle x,a₁,Q\{x,y},y,a₂,x attains that bound. One gateway survives any single deletion, making the graph 2-strong. Choosing a≥k−1 gives n≥d+k, while d+3<d+k for k≥4; increasing q makes d unbounded.
claims.witness: The explicit q+2 vertex cycle through both gateways and two A-vertices attains c(D)=d+3.
claims.search_method: Direct construction proof and exact checks over bounded q,a,k parameter grids.

claims.claim: The two-gateway example extends exactly as follows. For integers s≥2, q≥s+1, and a≥s, let Q be a bidirected q-vertex clique, let A be an independent a-vertex set, add every arc A→Q, and add arcs from Q to A precisely when their tail belongs to a fixed s-set S⊂Q. Then d=q−1, the strong vertex-connectivity is exactly s, and the circumference is q+s=d+s+1.
claims.evidence: Because Q\S is nonempty, its vertices have outdegree q−1, while A-vertices have q and S-vertices have q−1+a; hence d=q−1. Deleting fewer than s vertices leaves a gateway, a Q-vertex, and an A-vertex, and the surviving gateway joins all directions, so the remainder is strong. Deleting S leaves no path from Q\S to A, proving connectivity exactly s. Every cycle has at most s A-vertices by the predecessor injection into S, hence length at most q+s. Alternating the s gateways with s distinct A-vertices and then traversing Q\S gives a q+s cycle.
claims.witness: For enumerations S={s₁,…,s_s} and distinct a_i∈A, use s₁,a₁,…,s_s,a_s, followed by all vertices of Q\S and return to s₁.
claims.search_method: Exact degree, vertex-cut, predecessor, and constructive-cycle proof; checked 38 bounded parameter triples exactly.

claims.claim: For every k≥3 and h≥0 there is a 2-strong NO-instance whose order and circumference satisfy n=d+k+h and c(D)=d+k−1. For every k≥4 these instances can additionally have arbitrarily large d and strong vertex-connectivity exactly k−2.
claims.evidence: For k=3, bidirected K_{2,3+h} has d=2, n=5+h=d+k+h, connectivity at least two, and circumference 4=d+k−1. For k≥4, instantiate claim 7 with s=k−2, a=k−1+h, and arbitrary q≥k−1. Then d=q−1, n=q+a=d+k+h, connectivity is k−2, and c=q+s=d+k−1. Since q is arbitrary, d is unbounded, and the circumference remains one below the target.
claims.witness: The stated bipartite instance for k=3 and generalized gateway instance for k≥4 meet every equality exactly.
claims.search_method: Symbolic substitution into independently proved constructions plus exact checks for k=3–7 and several h,q values.

claims.claim: The target has a polynomial-time solution on semicomplete digraphs: such an input is YES exactly when n≥d+k, and a Hamiltonian directed cycle can be constructed when YES.
claims.evidence: Let C be a non-Hamiltonian cycle in a strong semicomplete digraph. If an outside z fits c_i→z→c_{i+1}, insert it. Otherwise, cyclic propagation shows z either is exclusively dominated by every C-vertex or exclusively dominates every C-vertex. Strongness forces both outside classes and an arc u→v from the first to the second; otherwise the first class could not reach C. Replacing any C-edge by c_i→u→v→c_{i+1} enlarges C. Repetition constructs a Hamiltonian cycle polynomially. Target inputs are 2-strong and hence strong, so a qualifying cycle exists exactly when its necessary size condition n≥d+k holds.
claims.witness: The iterative one-vertex or two-vertex insertion procedure terminates with an n-vertex directed cycle.
claims.search_method: Constructive proof of the strong-semicomplete Hamiltonicity lemma and exhaustive testing of all 59808 semicomplete digraphs through order five, including all 52528 strong cases.

claims.claim: Given any baseline cycle C with ℓ=|C|≥d+1, either ℓ≥d+k and C is a target witness, or r=d+k−ℓ satisfies 1≤r≤k−1 and the target reduces exactly to Connected Assignment Augmentation: find a perfect matching whose induced permutation has exactly one nontrivial cycle and at least ℓ+r nonfixed vertices.
claims.evidence: Arc edges plus zero-weight diagonals make every perfect matching a permutation. Its nonfixed permutation cycles are directed cycles of D; exactly one nontrivial permutation cycle therefore corresponds bijectively to one directed cycle, with its number of nonfixed vertices equal to the cycle length. A target cycle extends by diagonals to such a matching, and the reverse extraction is immediate. If the baseline is short, r=d+k−ℓ≥1 and ℓ≥d+1 gives r≤k−1. This is an exact parameter-preserving reformulation, though not an algorithm for the connected constraint.
claims.witness: Use successor edges of a directed cycle and diagonal edges elsewhere; conversely read the unique nontrivial permutation cycle from a feasible matching.
claims.search_method: Bijection and parameter-bound proof, exhaustively compared with direct cycle existence on every loopless digraph through four vertices.

claims.claim: For every loopless digraph D, the maximum number p(D) of vertices coverable by pairwise vertex-disjoint directed cycles is computable in polynomial time by maximum-weight bipartite perfect matching. Moreover c(D)≤p(D), so p(D)<d+k is a sound polynomial-time NO rule.
claims.evidence: A perfect matching of left and right vertex copies defines a permutation. Nonfixed permutation cycles use only arc edges and form pairwise vertex-disjoint directed cycles, while fixed points use zero-weight diagonals. Its weight is exactly the number of covered vertices. Conversely, any disjoint cycle packing extends with diagonals to a matching of equal weight. Thus maximum-weight perfect matching computes p(D) polynomially. Every single directed cycle is a packing, so c(D)≤p(D), establishing the NO rule.
claims.witness: The packing-to-permutation and permutation-to-packing maps preserve exactly the covered-vertex count.
claims.search_method: Formal weight-preserving bijection plus exhaustive equality checks between assignment and packing optima on every loopless digraph through four vertices.

claims.claim: The cycle-packing bound subsumes every independent-set predecessor certificate from the parent: p(D)≤n−|X|+|S| under that certificate's hypotheses. It is tight on the parent's bidirected complete multipartite, gateway, and strong semicomplete families.
claims.evidence: Across a vertex-disjoint cycle packing, map every covered x∈X to its predecessor. Independence and the entry condition place the predecessor in S, and disjointness makes the map injective. Hence at most |S| vertices of X and at most n−|X| outside vertices are covered. For a multipartite graph with 2d<n, take X as a largest part and S as its complement to obtain p≤2d, attained by the 2d-cycle; when 2d≥n, its Hamiltonian cycle attains n. Gateway graphs attain q+s under X=A, and strong semicomplete graphs attain n by a Hamiltonian cycle. Thus p=c in every listed family.
claims.witness: The maximum cycles from claims 3, 7, and 9 attain their respective packing upper bounds.
claims.search_method: Packing-wide predecessor injection and separate equality proofs for all three families; exact finite tests included.

claims.claim: The one-cycle constraint cannot be discarded even for 2-strong inputs: the bidirected Petersen digraph has d=3 and p(D)=10 but circumference c(D)=9. Consequently, for k=7 it is a NO-instance with n=d+k on which the matching relaxation attains the target threshold.
claims.evidence: Bidirecting the cubic Petersen graph gives d=3. Deleting any vertex leaves the undirected graph connected by the intact outer or inner 5-cycle and remaining spokes, hence the digraph remains strong. The five bidirected spokes form five disjoint directed 2-cycles covering all ten vertices, so p=10. A Hamiltonian cycle would use a positive even number of spokes. With two, their indices would have to be adjacent both on the outer 5-cycle and the inner step-two 5-cycle, impossible. With four, degree constraints force two disjoint 5-cycles. Thus c≤9, while the displayed nine-vertex cycle proves c=9. For k=7, d+k=n=10, so the target answer is NO although p reaches ten.
claims.witness: Using indices modulo five, a₁,a₂,a₃,a₄,b₄,b₂,b₀,b₃,b₁ is a directed 9-cycle; the five spoke 2-cycles witness p=10.
claims.search_method: Independent parity/degree proof and exact dynamic-programming enumeration of circumference, packing optimum, degrees, and vertex connectivity.

target_evidence: The exact source target asks for an f(k)n^{O(1)} algorithm on arbitrary 2-strong digraphs. The draft explicitly does not supply such an algorithm: Connected Assignment Augmentation is an exact reformulation whose one-cycle constraint remains unsolved, and the polynomial matching relaxation is insufficient by claim 13. The verified baseline algorithm, exact reformulations, upper-bound rule, tractable subclasses, and sharp obstruction families are nevertheless material correct progress. Therefore PARTIAL is accurate and the target is not fully resolved.
